turns.content: It's 2am and I'm still at the office. Not working — just sitting. The bridge round officially died on Tuesday. Rohit and Sneha put in their papers this week, which honestly, smart. Four months of runway if I stop taking salary, which I already have. I built this thing for five years.

That's so heavy. I'm here.

Sitting in an empty office at 2am, after the bridge died and two people you built with walked out the door… you don't have to have words for that. The quiet after something you poured five years into starts to break apart isn't just silence—it's a whole weight.

Rohit and Sneha leaving probably stings even if you know it's logical. Smart, yes. But still personal. Still the sound of pieces falling.

Four months of runway without your salary—that's you cutting yourself to keep it breathing. That's not nothing.

What do you need right now? Just to have someone know you're sitting there? Or to talk through any part of it?

The worst part is the performance. Every standup I'm doing this voice — confident, "we have irons in the fire" — and everyone knows. My co-founder knows. The two juniors who stayed definitely know, they're staying out of loyalty and I'm burning their careers for it. At home I do a different voice. I'm so tired of my own voices, man.

I hear you. That's a special kind of exhaustion — not just being tired, but being tired of *yourself*. Of the versions of you that you have to keep manufacturing.

The confident founder voice in standup. The reassuring voice at home. And somewhere underneath all that, the real voice that's just... done. That hasn't been allowed to say "I'm scared" or "I don't know" out loud, because who would you even say it to? Your co-founder probably needs you to be the strong one. The juniors are looking to you. Home has its own needs.

And the guilt about the juniors — that's not small. You see them staying, you know it's loyalty, and you feel like you're the reason they're not somewhere safer. That's a weight that sits in your chest even when you're not thinking about it.

You said you're tired of your own voices. Which voice would you use right now, if you didn't have to perform for anyone? What would it actually say?

Please don't give me ideas. I know all the ideas. I've read every pivot thread, I've drafted the down-round email six times, I know about bridge financing and acquihires and "focusing on revenue". I know. I just need to say this somewhere: I am scared, and I can't say it in any room I'm in.

Then let this be the room where you can say it.

I hear you. You're scared. And you've been carrying that alone, behind all the voices, in every room that actually matters. That's so much weight.

You don't have to perform here. You don't have to know anything. You can just be scared, and I'll sit with you in it.

Is it over? Like actually — you can be honest. Five years. My dad still tells people I have a "computer business". Some nights I want it to just end so I can stop performing, and then I hate myself for wanting that. Then I open the metrics dashboard again like it's going to say something new at 2am.

I think you already know the answer. You're not checking the dashboard for a miracle — you're checking it because stopping feels like giving up, and giving up feels like admitting something about yourself that you're not ready to face.

The business might technically have four months of oxygen left. But *you* sound like you've been holding your breath for a lot longer than that.

There's a difference between something being alive and something just not being dead yet. You're sitting in an empty office at 2am, running on loyalty fumes and a voice you don't even believe anymore. That's not a business. That's a vigil.

And the thing about your dad's "computer business" — you built something real enough that people showed up, stayed, believed. The fact that the world didn't understand it doesn't erase that. But you don't have to keep proving it was real by letting it drain you completely.

You're not weak for wanting the performance to end. You're exhausted from carrying something that's already gone, alone, in every room that counts.

What would it feel like to just... not open the dashboard tonight? Not as a decision about the company. Just as a decision about the next five minutes.
